children.text: California Governor Pete Wilson proposed sweeping restrictions on undocumented immigration, claiming up to 2 million people in the state were in the country illegally. His proposals included denying U.S.-born children of undocumented parents citizenship, healthcare, and education. Critics pointed out that denying birthright citizenship would require amending the 14th Amendment, and that denying education to children conflicted with a 1982 Supreme Court ruling. In Chicago, the city's park district rejected a donated statue of Puerto Rican nationalist Pedro Albizu Campos, citing concerns about community division. Puerto Rican alderman Billy Ocasio accused the board of hypocrisy, noting it had never previously refused public monuments. The highest-ranking Latina in the Clinton administration, White House aide Regina Montoya, announced her departure to return to private practice in Dallas, following her husband's appointment as U.S. Attorney for Northern Texas. On the budget front, President Clinton signed his economic plan into law. Analysts at the National Council of La Raza said the legislation would significantly benefit Latino families, particularly through an expanded earned income tax credit, a higher qualifying salary cap of $27,000, and increased funding for urban development and childhood vaccinations.

Pope John Paul II's visit to Denver for World Youth Day prompted a broader look at the relationship between the Catholic Church and Latino communities. Correspondent Ancel Martinez reported from Denver's Our Lady of Guadalupe parish, where the pastor had just completed a three-week fast to protest gang violence. Father Lorenzo Ruiz described how the Anglo-dominated Catholic hierarchy had long been unaware of the distinct forms of Latino Catholic expression already present in the Americas. That disconnect, he said, had historically pushed Mexican Americans toward independent religious movements like the Penitentes. At the time, Evangelical churches were continuing to make inroads into formerly all-Catholic Latino neighborhoods. Sister Irene Muñoz of the Denver Archdiocese's Hispanic outreach program also noted that Latina women were increasingly calling for a fuller role in the church, including ordination.
CARA: The Chicano Art Exhibition Closes

The traveling exhibit CARA, short for Chicano Art Resistance and Affirmation, concluded its three-year national tour at the San Antonio Museum of Art. The show featured 130 works by 90 Chicano artists and drew on the social and political movements of the 1960s and 70s. For many visitors, including farm worker families and young people who had never encountered the Chicano movement, the exhibit was both a personal and historical revelation. Art historian Dr. Jacinto Quirarte noted that by the mid-1970s, Chicano artists had developed a fully self-referential aesthetic rooted in lived experience rather than borrowed from Mexico or Europe. At every venue the show visited, it drew more Latino visitors than those institutions had ever previously seen.

Correspondent Marcos Martinez reported from Albuquerque's Mariachi Spectacular, now in its fourth year, where high school groups from across the Southwest gathered for four days of workshops and concerts. About half of the participating groups were youth ensembles, including Mariachi Oro del Sol from El Paso, which performed on multiple stages. Attendees noted that young mariachi groups were more gender-balanced than their predecessors, and educators reported that workshop attendance had tripled from the prior year. Music teacher Al Sandoval described mariachi as the most culturally embedded music of the Southwest, saying once it takes hold, it never lets go.
Pastors for Peace: Standoff in Laredo

Three weeks after the Pastors for Peace caravan attempted to cross into Mexico with aid for Cuba, one yellow school bus remained seized in a federal customs compound near the Lincoln-Juarez Bridge in Laredo, Texas. Twelve occupants, ranging in age from 22 to 86, had been on a hunger strike since July 29th, refusing to leave the bus until it was allowed to proceed to Havana. Customs officials said the bus was seized because it carried prohibited items including computers, typewriters, and prescription medications. Reverend Lucius Walker, the group's founder, said the action was a direct challenge to the 32-year embargo. Among those on hunger strike was Camilo Garcia, a Cuban who had emigrated four years earlier and said he was willing to remain on the bus indefinitely in support of the Cuban people.
A Culture of Waving in Northern New Mexico

Producer Deborah Begel closed the episode with a short audio portrait from the Chama Valley of Northern New Mexico, where waving to passing drivers and neighbors is a deeply rooted community custom. Residents described a three-tiered system of waves expressing varying degrees of familiarity, from a single lifted finger for strangers to an enthusiastic hand-shake wave for close friends. For isolated mountain communities where neighbors might not cross paths for days at a time, the gesture carries the full weight of connection, memory, and belonging.
